lessons.title: Why a cash reserve?
lessons.content: Profit on paper does not pay the bills — cash does. A reserve of 3–6 months of fixed costs lets your business survive late payments or a slow season without panic decisions.

question.prompt: Your fixed costs are 30,000 per month. What is a healthy minimum reserve?
question.explanation: 3 months × 30,000 = 90,000. That covers a typical late payment or slow quarter.

lessons.title: Risk vs. time horizon
lessons.content: Investments that can grow more, like ETFs, also swing more in the short term. The longer you can leave money untouched, the more short-term drops you can wait out.

question.prompt: You will need this money in 6 months. Which option fits best?
options: Keep it all as cash forever
question.explanation: With a short horizon, a market drop may not recover in time. Low-risk options protect money you need soon.

lessons.title: Don't put all eggs in one basket
lessons.content: Diversification means spreading money across different assets. When one falls, others may hold or rise, so the whole portfolio swings less.

options: A mix of deposit, bonds and a broad ETF
question.explanation: A broad ETF alone holds hundreds of companies, and mixing it with bonds and deposits reduces risk further.

lessons.title: Costs that lower your tax
lessons.content: Business tax is usually paid on profit, not revenue. Legitimate business costs reduce profit, so planning purchases with taxes in mind keeps more cash in the company.

question.explanation: Profit = revenue − deductible costs. That is the base for income tax.

lessons.title: Reinvesting in your business
lessons.content: Sometimes the best investment is your own company: a new machine or better marketing can raise revenue for years. Compare the expected extra profit with what the money would earn elsewhere.

question.prompt: A 20,000 machine adds 1,000 profit per month. How long until it pays for itself?
question.explanation: 20,000 ÷ 1,000 = 20 months. That is the payback period.
